content:
The Muon optimizer1 allows us to train LLMs faster. In comparison to AdamW, research results have shown speedups from 10%2 to 50%3. By now, Muon has gone beyond a research experiment and estabilished itself in large scale production training runs, such as DeepSeek-V44.
For diffusion transformers, the picture is less clear. Although this several papers started using Muon instead of Adam, I have found a lack of systematic studies comparing both optimizer. The goal of this post is to shed light on the benefits of Muon for training diffusion transformers through a set of experiments on the ImageNet dataset. We will start out by tuning the learning rate of Adam baseline, then evaluate several strategies to integrate Muon, and finally scale up the best found configurations for each optimizers to a 465M parameter model.
To keep the experiments self contained without any dependencies on external models, we will not use a VAE but instead directly predict in pixel space5.
Baseline The model used for this experiment is a modernized version of the DiT with AdaLN for timestep and class conditioning, using the SwiGLU activation, RoPE, and no bias parameters.
24 layers (DiT-L), width = 1024 Adam optimizer with beta=(0.9, 0.95) and no weight decay Batch size = 256 To save compute during learning rate sweeps, we are using a smaller proxy 31M parameter model with a width of 256 and the maximum update parameterization (muP)6 to later transfer the best found learning rate to the large target model. At a learning rate of 4e-4, training is already significantly faster than at a learning rate of 2e-4. However increasing the learning rate even further leads to unstable training.
Adam learning rate sweep on the small proxy model.
Introducing Muon Let’s start off with a quick recap of Muon. The key difference of Muon compared to Adam is the orthogonalization of gradient update matrices. Exact orthogonalization requires a singular value decomposition, which would massively slow down training when performed at every step. Instead, Muon only approximately orthogonalizes the updates using the iterative Newton-Schulz algorithm. A common theory why orthogonalization helps is that Adam’s update are generally low rank, and orthogonalization helps the optimizer explore more directions in the high dimensional parameters space.
We apply Muon only to the hidden layers in the transformer blocks. The patch embedding, output layer, timestep MLP and AdaLN modulation layers are still optimized using Adam.
Using Muon we have to choose between two methods for scaling the learning rate $\gamma$. One method, proposed by Moonshot AI, is to scale it such that the element-wise RMS of the update matches the RMS of Adam’s update using: $$ \gamma \leftarrow 0.2\gamma \sqrt{\max(\text{fan-in}, \text{fan-out})} $$ The advantage of this scaling is that it allows us to re-use the learning rate tuned for Adam. Since the FID curves were relatively uneven, I evaluated the training across 3 random seed. On average Muon reaches a 10% lower FID than Adam after 400k training steps on the small proxy model.
Muon with its update RMS matched to Adam evaluated on the small proxy model.
The learning rate scaling method originally proposed by Muon’s authors scales the update so that its RMS-to-RMS operator norm is bounded by the learning rate: $$ \gamma \leftarrow \gamma \sqrt{\frac{\text{fan-out}}{\text{fan-in}}} $$ Although this requires seperately tuning the learning rate for Muon, it enables learning rate transfer across model widths without any muP learning rate scaling7. And this is actually the original scaling method proposed by the Muon authors. With this scaling Muon requires a higher learning rate than Adam. The of thumb is that it should be 10x the Adam learning rate.
Muon outperform Adam across all the learning rates in the sweep on average over 3 random seeds. With a learning rate of 4e-4 the original scaling method (FID=69.9) slightly outperforms Moonshot’s method (FID=70.9). So we will use the original methods to scale up the model.
Muon learning rate sweep on the small proxy model using Muon’s original learning rate scaling. The black line shows the FID curve from the best Adam training run.
